attributes.colonial_era: Writers such as Louis-Marie Pouka and Sankie Maimo were educated by European missionary societies and argued for assimilation into European culture.
attributes.after_the_second_world_war: Writers such as Mongo Beti and Ferdinand Oyono analysed and criticised colonialism and rejected assimilation.
attributes.first_generation_of_novelists: Mongo Beti, René Philombe, Francis Bebey and Ferdinand Oyono, with a mission of close and critical analysis of colonisation.
attributes.other_older_writers: Guillaume Oyono-Mbia, Mbella Sonne Dipoko and Kenjo Jumbam.
attributes.critically_acclaimed_writers: Marcien Towa, Imbolo Mbue, Patrice Nganang, Calixthe Beyala, Bate Besong, Gaston-Paul Effa, Werewere Liking, Ba'bila Mutia, John Nkemngong Nkengasong, Bole Butake, Leonora Miano, Francis B. Nyamnjoh and Linus T. Asong.
attributes.honour: Sankie Maimo received the Grand prix de la mémoire at the 2016 Grand Prix of Literary Associations (GPLA).

attributes.author: Jean-Louis Njemba Medu
attributes.note: Sometimes considered the first novel by a Cameroonian author. It is a science fiction novel.
attributes.context: Among the first Cameroonians to write in French were Isaac Moumé Etia, who wrote short stories in the 1920s and 1930s, and Louis Pouka Mbague.

attributes.early_writing: Sans haine et sans amour (1953), a short story, was his first significant writing.
attributes.main_themes: A commitment to fighting colonialism, open or hidden.
attributes.main_basse: He published Main basse sur le Cameroun in 1972. It was banned in France, and in 1976 he and his editor François Maspéro won its release through the courts.
attributes.return: After 32 years of exile he returned to Cameroon and wrote La France contre l'Afrique, retour au Cameroun (1993).
attributes.education: Studied at Aix-en-Provence and then at the Sorbonne in Paris, and took the agrégation in 1966.
